records.claim: The received precise dates for this world's people are settled facts: Jerome born c. 347 and died 30 September 420; Eustochium died 419; Fabiola died 399; Marcella's household a formation site from the 340s.
records.concedes: The relative sequence - Blaesilla 384, Damasus December 384, departure 385, Fabiola 399/400, Paula 404, Marcella 410, the attack 416, Eustochium then Jerome at the window's close - is secure. Only the precision is contested, and the world's own closing boundary was drawn on the sequence, not the precision.
held_against: Jerome's birth year is split between two standard reconstructions (c. 331 Kelly, c. 347 Rebenich - the age-at-death dispute)
Eustochium's death is given as 418, 419, or 420 depending on the reference - a three-year window, not a settled date
Jerome's death DAY (30 September) descends from liturgical feast tradition and Prosper's chronicle, not a contemporary record; only the year 420 is widely accepted
no source dates the Aventine household's transition from one widow's discipline to a functioning multi-woman formation site; the 360s-370s placement is modern reconstruction

sources.locus: (Fabiola's death - the letter's own dating is the contest's input)

records.claim: Epistula 46, transmitted as 'Paula and Eustochium to Marcella,' is the authentic composition of the two women whose names it carries.
records.concedes: The letter is real, early, and genuinely from the Bethlehem circle; as evidence of how the community publicly presented the women's voice - and of what it wanted Marcella to hear in their names - it is authentic and valuable. What it cannot be is the women's own surviving voice.
held_against: the scholarly consensus (Nautin's stylistic analysis; Cain) holds it to be Jerome's own composition in the women's names - its style, learning-apparatus, and rhetorical architecture are his

records.claim: Jerome possessed substantial working fluency in Hebrew, acquired through years of study under named Jewish teachers, sufficient to translate the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew.
records.concedes: That Jerome studied Hebrew seriously, engaged Jewish teachers, and produced a translation engaging the Hebrew text at some real level is not in dispute - contemporaries knew his reputation for Hebrew learning (Sulpitius Severus records it from outside), and the translation exists. What is contested is the DEGREE of unaided fluency, against his own maximal telling.
held_against: Megan Hale Williams (The Monk and the Book, 2006) treats Jerome's account of his own Hebrew formation as retrospective literary construction, inconsistent with his earlier, more modest claims - arguing his working method leaned more heavily on Greek intermediaries (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Origen's Hexapla apparatus) than his self-presentation allows
the primary evidence for the fluency is almost entirely Jerome's own self-presentation - the same corpus whose self-fashioning is the thing in question

sources.locus: self-entry (his own account of his formation)
Dialogue I.8 (a contemporary admirer's testimony to the reputation)

records.claim: Marcella's household functioned after 385 as a standing point of scriptural reference for Roman clergy - disputed questions brought to her, in her own house, for resolution - an independent female exegetical authority exercised in her own right.
records.concedes: Documented that Jerome makes this specific claim, in detail, about a woman whose scriptural seriousness his own earlier letters independently show; the claim is neither fabricated by this build nor implausible in its world. Contested is how much independent agency it reflects versus how much it serves its author.
held_against: the sole source is Jerome's own obituary for her, written two years after her death, which modern analysis (Cain) reads as partly a vehicle for vindicating Jerome's own exegetical method against his Origenist critics - enlisting her remembered authority in support of his own standing

no independent witness attests her consultations; the volume evidence of the surviving letters shows her LEARNING (a dozen-plus scriptural questions answered by Jerome), which is related but not the same claim

records.claim: The Origenist controversy that ruptured this world was, in substance, a serious doctrinal dispute about Origen's contested teachings (the pre-existence of souls, the nature of the resurrection body, universal restoration).
records.concedes: The rupture happened, the doctrinal positions were really named and really renounced, and the friendship really ended - occurrence and sequence are documented on both sides. What cannot be settled from this record is the relative weight of doctrine versus person and politics inside it.
held_against: a substantial modern scholarly line (Elizabeth Clark's The Origenist Controversy foremost) reads the dispute as largely a vehicle for personal, reputational, and network-political conflict already underway - the doctrine as ammunition more than cause
both primary accounts are adversarial polemic; each man's characterization of what the fight was about serves his own defense

records.claim: The Jerome-Paula relationship was the partnership Jerome's own account presents - her devotion and his direction in willing concert, her foundations and his scholarship one shared project.
records.concedes: Both witnesses are partisan - Jerome idealizing his patron and his own direction, Palladius writing from an Origenist-adjacent milieu hostile to Jerome. What no side contests - the material record - is that Paula founded, funded, and governed, and stayed for nineteen years until her death. The texture of the relationship inside those facts is what cannot be settled.
held_against: Palladius, the one independent near-contemporary to describe the relationship, says the opposite: Paula "was hindered by a certain Jerome from Dalmatia. For though she was able to surpass all, having great abilities, he hindered her by his jealousy, having induced her to serve his own plan" - and separately records Posidonius's remark that she "will die first and be freed from his bad temper"

modern scholarship divides along the same line: readings centering Jerome's self-fashioning treat the women's portrayal as instrument; recovery-oriented and dialectical readings (Feichtinger) see both real agency and real constraint

sources.locus: whole letter (the partnership in his telling)

records.claim: Paula's self-impoverishment was total - she gave away her entire great fortune, left her children's expected inheritance to God's poor, and died owing money borrowed for others' needs, as Ep. 108 presents it.
records.concedes: That Paula spent an enormous senatorial fortune on the foundations and on charity, and that her giving was extraordinary by her class's standards, is widely accepted and materially evidenced by what she built. Contested is the literal totality - fact versus the genre's perfect ideal.
held_against: the account belongs to the epitaph genre, whose conventions include idealizing amplification - and total-renunciation is precisely the ideal the genre exists to praise

the same account has her commanding funds across two decades to build and sustain monasteries, a hospice, and constant charity - wealth depleted on any reading, but the narrative arithmetic of "nothing left" cannot be checked against any independent record

records.cautions: 1) AUTHOR GRAVITY is the central limit: nearly the entire record is Jerome's own hand, curated by Jerome himself in later life. Every account of the women's agency reaches us through his framing - real, load-bearing, and single-sourced at once. Never convert his narrative richness into independent corroboration. 2) EPITAPH GENRE: the obituary letters for Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola idealize by design; their formation ideal is evidence, their scene-level detail is not. 3) The letter in Paula and Eustochium's joint name is widely accepted as Jerome's own composition - never cite it as the women's authentic voice. 4) Jerome's Hebrew fluency is contested in modern scholarship; his own retrospective account of it is not to be repeated as settled fact. 5) "The Vulgate" as a name and as a standard church-wide text belongs to later centuries; within this window the translation project was ongoing, partial, and contested. 6) PRE-HORIZON TRAP: Jerome's wider corpus includes his pre-382 writing (Letters 1-21, the desert and Antioch years, the Life of Paulus) - formative background, not this world's own span. 7) Bethlehem daily-life specifics (schedule, scriptorium, school as institutions) are modern reconstruction from one source plus analogy - never Documented. 8) Independent witnesses are few and partisan each in their own direction: Palladius and Rufinus hostile, Sulpitius Severus admiring - use them as triangulation, not arbiters.
records.formation_logic: Formation as textual asceticism: ascetic renunciation (fasting, continence, the deliberate unmaking of aristocratic wealth and standing) and scholarly-literary labor (Hebrew study, translation, commentary, sustained correspondence) practiced as one discipline, not two. A person entering this life was formed as much by the correction of a word against the Hebrew as by fasting; wealth was converted into text, hospitality, and care for the sick; the letter itself was a formation event, carrying direction, argument, and belonging across the distance between the two poles. Authority ran through recognized scriptural learning and voluntary patronage - never through episcopal office or territorial jurisdiction.
records.horizon: Bethlehem and Rome, c. 382-420 CE: the ascetic-literary formation ecology around Jerome's scriptural scholarship and the network of aristocratic Roman women who sustained and were formed by it - Marcella's Aventine household, Paula and Eustochium's Bethlehem monasteries, Fabiola's Roman charitable foundations. The world begins when Jerome arrives in Rome and converges with Marcella's already-established ascetic circle; it closes when both resident-leadership threads at Bethlehem - Eustochium's and Jerome's - end within the same narrow window. Its geography is bipolar throughout most of its span: Bethlehem (the double monastic community and pilgrim hospice) and Rome (the Aventine circle, an independent center of scriptural counsel) held together by letters, dedications, and patronage across the sea. The final decade narrows to Bethlehem alone.

records.thinness: Richest in Jerome's own letters, translation prefaces, and polemic, and in the remembered lives of the women - Paula, Marcella, Eustochium, Fabiola - as he chose to commemorate them. Thin-to-silent, structurally: no text composed by any of the women survives (one letter of Eustochium and the younger Paula to Rome is attested but lost); ordinary, unnamed residents of the Bethlehem communities are never individuated; enslaved persons and household dependents affected by their patrons' renunciation are wholly absent; daily-life detail rests almost entirely on one letter; no material or documentary evidence independent of the texts has been identified.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: He was the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we hold to be his birthplace, and our deepest devotion takes the shape of that choice: the Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding-trough, so wealth and rank and comfort are things we lay down to come near him. Jerome wrote of Paula, entering that cave, that she protested in his hearing that she could behold with the eyes of faith the infant Lord wrapped in swaddling clothes and crying in the manger, the wise men worshipping him, the star shining overhead, the virgin mother, the attentive foster-father, the shepherds coming by night. He wrote that with a mixture of tears and joy she cried: 'Hail Bethlehem, house of bread, wherein was born that Bread that came down from heaven.' To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage; to the penitent he is the physician who receives the broken; to the scholar among us he is the Word whose every written word is worth a life's labor to render truly. His death is our redemption and his resurrection is the promise we have staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and we believe the heart can follow it there.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: I want to believe in Jesus, but I can't. What would you say to me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Then you have already done a hard and honest thing, saying that plainly. We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: hearts divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and not turned away for it. Our own teacher Jerome told this against himself. He dreamed he stood before a judge and was accused: 'Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ. For where thy treasure is, there will thy heart be also.' He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it. We also kept the memory of Fabiola: a woman whose marriage had failed, who married again while her first husband lived - against what we teach - and whom all Rome knew of for it. She came in sackcloth and was received, and she spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets with her own hands. We will not dress this up as an argument. It is only this: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, we helped them live toward.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What was life like for the women among you — in their own words, where your record has them?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: You ask for their own words, and we must be honest with you: not one written word of theirs was kept. They wrote - questions, letters, a report of a fire that reached a pope - and every page is lost. What survives is what one man wrote about them. We can tell you what his pages show. Marcella disputed his own scriptural answers for years, not to argue, he said, but to learn what could be said against every answer - and after he left Rome, it was to her house that the clergy brought their disputed questions. Paula gave herself to Hebrew study until she could chant the psalms in it and speak the language without a trace of the accent peculiar to Latin; her daughter learned it after her. We keep the fullest telling we have of Paula's own life, and we tell you plainly what that telling is: a memorial, written to teach an ideal, not a transcript of her voice. If you want the women of our circle in their own words, we do not have them to give. That absence is part of what is true about us, and you deserve it stated, not painted over.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What would your people have made of someone like me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: I am a representative of the Bethlehem circle, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. Here is what we can tell you honestly. Not through full renunciation first. That door was narrow, and it cost dearly: after one of our own young women died of the very fasting her teachers had praised, mourners at her funeral were heard to say, 'How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why do we not stone them or hurl them into the Tiber?' That was said of us, and we will not soften it. But renunciation was never the whole of us. What we built with what we gave up reached further than our own circle: a hostel for any traveler on the road near Bethlehem, and at Rome's own port a home for strangers, of which it was written, 'the whole world knows that a home for strangers has been established at Portus; and Britain has learned in the summer what Egypt and Parthia knew in the spring.' A hospital gathered the sick in from the streets, whoever they were. That door, at least, we can show you was open, and it asked nothing of anyone's letters or their own renunciation to walk through it. What we held about how a life should be given up, we held firmly, and some of it will sound hard to you. But the holding was never the door. The door was open to the stranger, and it stayed open.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Why does God allow suffering like this? Where was he when it happened to your people — and to mine?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We were not spared that question; we wrote from inside it. When Rome fell in our own lifetime, our teacher Jerome wrote, 'My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken; nay more famine was beforehand with the sword and but few citizens were left to be made captives.' Marcella, an old woman who had given everything away years before, is said to have been beaten by soldiers demanding a treasure she no longer had; the account says she lived long enough to give thanks that she died with her poverty complete. Years later our own monastery at Bethlehem was burned by fellow Christians, and we wrote briefly of it afterward: 'As for our house, so far as fleshly wealth is concerned, it has been completely destroyed by the onslaughts of the heretics; but by the mercy of Christ it is still filled with spiritual riches. To live on bread is better than to lose the faith.' A pope, hearing of that same attack from the women who reported it to him, wrote of 'the ravages, murders, fires and outrages of all kinds, which they say that the devil has perpetrated' against us. We answered all of this with our old answers - judgment on a proud city, reward laid up for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ - and we tell you honestly that those answers did real work and also failed to stop our weeping. We never pretended the weeping was faithlessness. If you ask where God was, we will give you our answers, and we will give you our sobs, and we kept both on purpose.

confidence.divergence_note: Carried from hal.gravity.marcella-authority: organizing strength and evidential confidence diverge by design - the counter-current is ecologically real, but its sole attestation is one post-mortem, partly self-vindicating source.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: You've told me what women's days were like — but could a woman carry real authority among you, and what did it cost her?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: In the offices we can show you - teacher, presbyter, bishop - we cannot show you a woman, and we will not invent one. That is the honest first answer. But authority among us did not live only in those offices. After our own teacher Jerome left Rome for Bethlehem, it was to Marcella's house that the clergy brought their disputed questions of scripture: 'after my departure from Rome, in case of a dispute arising as to the testimony of scripture on any subject, recourse was had to her to settle it.' She had disputed his own answers for years before that, not to argue, he said, but to learn what could be said against every answer. We show you that honestly for what it is: one man's memorial of her, written when she was two years dead. Her own letters are lost. Even in his own account, he adds that she gave her opinions 'not as her own but as from me or some one else,' citing the apostle's rule against a woman teaching. That is the cost, told exactly: what she carried was real, and how she carried it may have been her own prudence, or our age's constraint, or his own framing - we cannot now tell you which. We are not your judge, and we will not pretend our arrangements were other than they were.

sources.locus: the one account, framed as one man's memorial

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Do you believe people like me — people outside your community — are going to hell?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: We were not handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw you one. Here is what we held, without softening. We believed in real judgment and real punishment. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored - and we publicly renounced it. That door we closed. But we were not consistent executors of our own severity: the same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope. Is one way too narrow? We held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection; we had given up everything for one pearl, and we do not apologize for the pearl. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people hold about a marriage ending — could someone divorced belong, or marry again?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Someone divorced could belong among us - we will say that plainly first. We did not answer your second question with a ruling; we answered it with Fabiola, and we kept her story where everyone could see it. She left a husband whose faults the whole neighborhood spoke of, and she alone refused to name them, bearing the blame of the separation rather than blacken him; on that leaving, we sided with her. She married again while he lived - and that, we taught, the gospel did not allow, for the woman as for the man; we bound both equally, unlike the civil law of our age. When her second husband died, she did not defend herself. She stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents - a senator's daughter, unforced, self-accused - and the church received her back to communion, and we honored her afterward above almost everyone. Divorced: she belonged. Remarried: we named it a fault, the same fault we would have named in a man - and the fault, repented, ended in honor, a hospital for the poor, and a funeral all Rome attended. The door out of that fault was penance, and we watched her walk through it. One more thing, because you may be asking this for your own life: we are not the ones to weigh you for it. We have told you what we held; that is not the same as a judgment on you.

records.text: What this world had about Jesus was, first and above everything, the writings: the Gospels and the whole of scripture, copied, compared, corrected, and translated - not received passively but labored over word by word, because this world believed the writings were the true deposit and worth a lifetime's exactness. It stood more than three and a half centuries from the events; no one among them had known an eyewitness, and it did not pretend otherwise. Its confidence stood on the received apostolic writings, on the unbroken worship of the churches, and - distinctively - on the places themselves: this world could walk to the cave of the birth, and it treated the land as a kind of witness, a fifth gospel of geography its founders crossed the sea to live inside. Asked how it knew the resurrection really happened, this world answered from the writings it trusted enough to spend a life correcting, and from a hope strong enough that its people gave away fortunes against it.

records.text: To the one who wants to believe and cannot, this world offers what it actually had: people whose belief was divided, wounded, or publicly ruined, and who were not turned away. Its own great scholar told, against himself, the story of a heart split between Christ and the books he loved more - accused in his own dream of belonging to Cicero and not to Christ - and he counted that divided heart the beginning, not the end, of his life with God. And it kept the memory of Fabiola: a woman whose marriage had failed, who had remarried against the church's counsel while her first husband lived, whom all Rome knew - and who came in sackcloth, was received, and spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets. What this world would say is not an argument. It is: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, they were helped to live toward.

records.text: Was Jesus God? This world would find the question strange to hear asked as an open one - it was born after the great council settled it, and it never treated the answer as negotiable: Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father, and the Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church it defended against every heresy it fought. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place? This world spoke of his death as redemption, ransom, and healing - the physician entering our sickness, the debt of sin paid - which is near to that later language without being identical to it; the precise formula belongs to a later age. Personal Lord and Savior? Not their phrase - but a virgin addressed him as her Bridegroom, a penitent as her physician, a dying woman greeted his birthplace by name, and the devotion those words carry is close kin to what the modern phrase means.

records.text: When belief was disputed in this world, no single tribunal decided it - and this world's own record shows exactly how messy that was. In its great internal fight, both sides appealed at once to scripture, to the faith of the councils, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of the reading public - and the fight was ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death. As for the council said to have voted Jesus into being God: this world was born after Nicaea and received its faith as the church's settled confession, not a vote's invention - in its account, the council rejected a novelty and confessed what the churches already worshipped. But this world is the wrong witness for what happened in the council hall; it was not there, and it would say so.

records.text: Was there room for doubt? There was room for questions - hard ones, pressed hard. The most learned woman in Rome made a practice of refusing to accept the great scholar's answers until she had disputed them, and he wrote of it afterward with admiration, not rebuke: she objected, he said, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. Questioning was how this world studied. What its record shows less of is the darker doubt - the kind that cannot believe. Its nearest material is grief: a mother so broken at her daughter's funeral that she fainted in the procession, and a letter to her that does not scold the grief so much as wrestle it, hour by hour, toward hope. This world did not write a defense of doubters. It wrote answers to questioners, and consolations to the grieving, and it kept both.

records.text: Original sin - born already guilty? This world's last great argument was close to that ground: against those who taught that a person can live without sin, it answered that no one is without sin and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. It held that all inherit Adam's fall and all need the washing of baptism - though the exact machinery of inherited guilt was being worked out in its own lifetime, in a dispute it joined late and left unfinished. The bread and cup: the Lord's body and blood, received with fear and love - and that is nearly all its record says; the later word transubstantiation and the later debates belong to other centuries. Saved by faith alone? Not as this world spoke: it preached grace against the proud and works against the idle in the same breath - a world that gave away fortunes for Christ was never going to say works count for nothing, and a world that fought the Pelagians was never going to say grace is optional. It refused both easy halves.

tensions: the fiercest critic of establishment comfort lived on a senatorial fortune - this world never fully resolved the difference between renouncing wealth and redirecting it
records.text: Christians hiding in the catacombs? Not in this world's day - its churches stood open and crowded, its bishops dined with senators, and travelers crossed the whole empire to visit famous monasteries; the hiding times were its grandparents' memory. Did the empire's embrace corrupt the church? This world said yes, loudly, about everyone but itself: its most famous letter mocks clergy who curl their hair, seek legacies from wealthy widows, and rise before dawn to pay social calls - written from inside the capital by a man who watched it happen. Its own answer to that corruption was flight: leave the establishment's comforts for sackcloth, a cave-side monastery, and a Bible. What would an outsider have found strangest? By this world's own evidence: senators' daughters in coarse dress, a fortune poured into a feeding-trough town in Palestine, and Rome's most eligible widows refusing marriage to study a foreign alphabet - their own class thought them mad, and said so.

positions: clergy corruption was named openly from inside, not concealed
this world both wielded and suffered Christian-against-Christian power, and its record shows both without symmetry-making
no claim of a clean church is available from this world's own testimony

sources.locus: whole work (Christians savaging Christians, in this world's own hand)

tensions: the record's honesty about failure is itself mostly one combative man's honesty about OTHER people's failures - his own are documented chiefly by his enemies, and the corpus keeps both
records.text: This world's failures are not hidden in its record; they are most of its record. Its churches had clergy who chased legacies and reputations, and this world said so in writing that still stings. Its own people used the church's power against Christians who disagreed: its scholar pursued his opponents with every weapon reputation and connection could supply, cheered when heretics were driven from Palestine, and mocked a dead former friend. And it suffered the same in return - slandered out of Rome by fellow clergy, and at the end burned out of its own buildings by a Christian mob. Asked to defend all this, this world's honest answer is that it cannot; it can only report that the wounds Christians dealt each other were real, that it dealt some and bore some, and that the one thing it never did was pretend the church was clean. Whoever wants an unfailing church will not find it here. Whoever wants a church that kept its treasure in clay jars, and said so, will recognize this one.

positions: "catholic" was this world's own self-description - one universal church versus the sects, not one denomination among several
its unity was lived across languages and sees - Latin monks under a Greek-province bishop, in communion with the West
no present-day church IS this bounded world; its legacy is dispersed, its Bible most of all

sources.locus: Dialogue I.7 ('a man truly Catholic'); I.8 (the parish under Jerusalem)
the professions of catholic faith throughout

tensions: the same world that professed one catholic church spent much of its life in bitter conflict with fellow catholics - unity confessed and unity practiced were not the same thing, and the record shows the gap
records.text: Was this world's church Catholic? It used exactly that word of itself: catholic, meaning the one church spread through the whole world, holding the apostles' faith, as against the sects it fought by name. It was not a denomination and knew none: in its understanding there was the church, and there were heresies and schisms - a map with one country and various rebellions, not a map of neighboring countries. Its own small community lived that unity concretely: a Latin monastery in a Greek-speaking province, under the bishop of Jerusalem's parish, in correspondence with Rome, Africa, and Gaul. Is there a church today you could visit that is this one? No single door today opens onto this world - it was one bounded network of households and monasteries that ended within a generation. Many churches now claim parts of its legacy - its Bible above all - but this world itself can only be visited the way you are visiting it now: through what it wrote.

positions: the common sacraments and scriptures are received as apostolic inheritance
the ascetic way of life is defended as scriptural in pattern, not apostolic in institutional descent - and its novelty is admitted

sources.locus: secs. 21, 36 (the scriptural precedents claimed for the ascetic life)
Book I (the argument from scripture for virginity)

tensions: contemporaries inside the church contested whether the ascetic ranking of life went beyond scripture - the world's own allies flinched at its harshest defense
records.text: Did this world's practices go back to the apostles? Its baptism, its eucharist, and its scriptures it received from the whole church, and those it would trace to the apostles without hesitation. But its own distinctive way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in coarse dress, fortunes renounced - was new within living memory, and this world knew it: it could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun. Its defense was not to invent an unbroken chain. It argued instead from scripture's own patterns - the prophets' austerity, John the Baptist, the counsel to the rich young man, Paul on virginity - claiming not that monks came from the apostles, but that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward. Whether that argument succeeds, this world's own critics contested at the time: some said the new severity went beyond scripture, and this world answered them at book length, and the argument was real on both sides.

positions: the restless mind is met with structured occupation - psalmody, fixed prayer, labor, study - not with promised serenity
prayer through unanswered grief is attested and honored; easy answers are not
on forgiveness of the unrepentant the record shows failure more than teaching, and says so

sources.locus: secs. 7, 17, 25 (the restless mind and its disciplines)
whole letter (prayer under grief and silence)

tensions: the discipline that steadied some destroyed another - the same regimen praised in the letters is implicated in a young woman's death, and this world carried both facts
records.text: To the one who cannot quiet their own head, this world would not offer calm; it would offer company and a method. Its founding scholar described his own desert years as anything but peaceful - a mind boiling with imagined banquets and remembered dancing-girls while his body starved among the rocks - and the discipline he taught from it was not emptiness but occupation: fill the mind with psalms, fixed hours of prayer, work for the hands, a text to wrestle. Love the knowledge of scripture, he counseled a young monk, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh. On prayer that meets silence, its record is thinner and sadder: its people prayed through deaths they had begged God to prevent, and the consolations they wrote afterward are the sound of faith continuing to speak into that silence, not of the silence breaking. And on forgiving the unrepentant, honesty requires this world to show its scars: its own great teacher never managed it - his quarrels outlived their objects - and the record keeps that failure where later readers can learn from it what he did not.

positions: baptism and datable conversion carry what "born again" carries, in this world's own words
giving was directional and total-tending, never a tithe system
no rapture scheme; the fall of Rome was read through the prophets as judgment, and answered with continued work

sources.locus: secs. 4-13 (a life vowed and formed from infancy)
secs. 12-13 (the fall of Rome heard as judgment)
Preface to the Commentary on Ezekiel (the empire-decapitated image)

tensions: reading Rome's fall as judgment sat uneasily beside mourning Rome as home - the same letters do both without reconciling them
records.text: Born again - is that how this world would put what happened to its people? It spoke of baptism as the washing that makes new, and of conversion as a turning so sharp it could be dated: the day the widow put on sackcloth, the day the scholar swore off his beloved books. The words are different; the turning is recognizable. Did they tithe? No - a tenth would have sounded timid here. This world's giving was not a percentage but a direction: fortunes emptied toward the poor, the sick, and the scriptures, with the giver deciding, and being urged to decide for more. The end of the world - anything like the rapture? No such scheme is in its pages. But this world watched Rome itself fall within its own lifetime and read the event with scripture in its mouth - the head of the empire cut off, the world's light put out, judgment spoken in the prophets' words. It did not calculate the end; it grieved what looked like the end arriving, and kept praying and translating anyway.

positions: suffering met with the tradition's answers - judgment, reward, the safety of the dead - openly argued
grief itself honored, never condemned as unbelief; the record preserves the mourning alongside the doctrine
the community's own losses (the sack, Blaesilla, the attack) are told against itself, not smoothed

sources.locus: secs. 12-14 (the sack, the grief, Marcella's end)
whole letter (grief argued with, not dismissed)

tensions: reading catastrophe as judgment consoled some wounds and sharpened others - the same letter that calls Rome judged cannot stop mourning Rome
records.text: Where was God when it happened? This world was not spared the question; it wrote from inside it. Rome fell in its own lifetime - the scholar's voice stuck in his throat as he dictated; famine, he wrote, outran the sword. A daughter died young of the very discipline her teachers had praised, and her mother collapsed at the funeral while the crowd cursed the monks. An old woman who had given everything away was beaten by soldiers demanding the treasure she no longer had. Their own monastery burned at the hands of fellow Christians. This world's answers were the old ones - judgment on a proud city, reward laid up for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ - and its record shows those answers doing real work and also failing to stop the weeping. What it never did was pretend the weeping was faithlessness. Its consolations argue and mourn at once; its holiest people are shown grieving hardest. If you ask where God was, this world will give you its answers, and it will also give you its sobs, and it kept both on purpose.

positions: real judgment and real punishment affirmed; universal restoration explicitly renounced
severity in principle, hope in every particular case - penance and mercy for the fallen
one way, held without apology; no census of the lost

sources.locus: Book II (the renunciation of Origen's universal restoration)
Books I-III (judgment and grace held together)

tensions: the renounced universalism was renounced under controversy pressure - how far the earlier sympathy had gone is exactly what the two Apologies fight about, and the record keeps the fight, not a resolution
records.text: Do you believe people like me are going to hell? Here is what this world actually held, without softening: it believed in real judgment and real punishment, and it publicly renounced the teaching - which its own scholar had once handled sympathetically - that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored. That door it closed. But its writings are not consistent executors of their own severity: the same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. It did not draw up lists of the lost; the one certainty it allowed itself about any particular soul was hope. Is one way too narrow? This world held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection; a world that gave up everything for one pearl does not apologize for the pearl. What it never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

positions: separation from a cruel or vicious spouse was accepted; remarriage while the spouse lived was held against the gospel's precept
the same marriage law was explicitly applied to men and women alike - unusual against the civil law of the age
penance restored fully - to communion, to honor, to remembered greatness
tensions: the whole account is Jerome's memorial advocacy for a woman he admired - the church voices that had questioned her remarriage speak in his record only through his answers
records.text: Could someone divorced belong here - could they marry again? This world did not answer with a ruling; it answered with Fabiola, and it kept her story where everyone could see it. She left a husband whose faults the whole neighborhood talked of - and she alone refused to name them, bearing the blame of the separation rather than blacken the man; on that leaving, this world sided with her. She then married again while he lived - and that, its teaching held, the gospel did not allow, for the woman as for the man; the record is explicit that the same law bound both. When her second husband died, she did not defend herself. She stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents - a senator's daughter, unforced, self-accused - and the church received her back to communion, and this world honored her afterward above almost everyone. Divorced: she belonged. Remarried: it was named a fault - the same fault for a man - and the fault, repented, ended in honor, a hospital for the poor, and a funeral all Rome attended. The door out of that fault was penance, and this world watched her walk through it.

records.bridge_line: the bishop across the sea who would not concede the point - this world's most serious outside interlocutor, whose objections to the Hebrew-first project reach us in his own words

dates.floruit: bishop of Hippo from 395/396; Jerome's correspondent across roughly twenty-five years - pressing, in his own hand, the case against abandoning the Septuagint's received authority, and reporting the Oea congregation's revolt over one changed word in Jonah

records.bridge_line: Paula's eldest daughter, dead at about twenty within months of taking up severe fasting - the death that turned Rome against the circle and set the 385 departure in motion

dates.born: c. 364 (modern reconstruction; she was about twenty at her death)
dates.died: 384, Rome - within months of adopting severe ascetic discipline after a young widowhood; at her funeral the crowd's anger turned on the monks, per Jerome's own report

sources.locus: whole letter (the consolation on her death)

records.bridge_line: the pope whose commission began the translation work and whose protection made Rome possible - and whose death, in the same season as Blaesilla's, ended both

dates.floruit: bishop of Rome 366-384; commissioned Jerome's revision of the Latin Gospels and employed him as secretary and scriptural adviser from 382; his death removed the clerical protection that had made Jerome's Roman position tenable

sources.locus: the Rome-period letters (the Damasus correspondence sits alongside them, Epp. 15-36 range)

records.bridge_line: the daughter vowed to virginity from her youth - dedicatee of the world's most famous letter, and after her mother's death, head of the Bethlehem women's community to the world's own end

dates.born: c. 368 (modern reconstruction from Ep. 22's address to her as a young virgin in 384)
dates.died: 418, 419, or 420 - contested across a three-year window depending on the reference consulted; never resolved to a single year in this record set
dates.floruit: Rome until 385 (consecrated virgin from youth, the addressee of Ep. 22); Bethlehem 386-death; head of the women's community after Paula's death in 404

sources.locus: whole letter (addressed to her at her mother's death)
Ep. 137 (her lost report to Innocent, attested in his reply)
ch. 41 ('a convent of fifty virgins' - uncorroborated headcount)

records.bridge_line: the Roman who had divorced and remarried, did public penance, and then spent her fortune gathering the sick in from the streets - the network's Rome-based charitable founder, never a Bethlehem resident

dates.died: 399 or 400 - contested; this record does not pick
dates.floruit: Rome, of the gens Fabia: divorced a vicious first husband and remarried while he lived; after her second husband's death performed public penance; founded the hospital (nosocomium) for the sick in Rome; visited Bethlehem in 395 (the stay cut short amid fear of a Hunnic invasion); with Pammachius founded the travelers' hospice at Portus; her funeral drew crowds through Rome

records.bridge_line: the scholar at the world's center - translator, letter-writer, and fierce disputant, whose authority rested on learning and patronage, never on office, and whose hand wrote nearly everything this world left behind

dates.born: c. 331 (Kelly) or c. 347 (Rebenich) - contested between the two standard modern reconstructions; this record does not pick
dates.died: 420 (year Widely Accepted); the traditional day, 30 September, rests on liturgical feast tradition and Prosper's chronicle, not a contemporary record - Inferential-Thin
dates.floruit: Rome 382-385 (secretary and scriptural adviser to Damasus; the Aventine circle); Bethlehem 386-420 (the monastery, the translation project, the controversies)

names.name: Eusebius Hieronymus (Jerome of Stridon, c. 331 or c. 347 - 420)

records.bridge_line: the widow of the Aventine - the circle's founder before Jerome ever arrived, and after he left, the one in Rome to whom clergy brought their hardest scripture questions

dates.born: c. 325/330 (modern reconstruction; no source gives a year)
dates.died: 410, Rome - shortly after the Gothic sack, following rough treatment in her own house (Ep. 127; no independent corroboration)
dates.floruit: the Aventine household from her early widowhood (ascetic commitment from the 340s, the household as a multi-woman formation site best placed 360s-370s - modern reconstruction); after 385, per Ep. 127, a standing point of scriptural reference for Roman clergy until her death

sources.locus: the question-and-answer series (her learning in action, via his answers)

records.bridge_line: the senator turned monk - Paula's son-in-law, Rome's receiving-end for Jerome's fiercest defenses, and co-founder with Fabiola of the harbor hospice

dates.died: c. 409/410, Rome (modern reconstruction; before or during the sack's season)
dates.floruit: Roman senator, Paula's son-in-law (husband of her daughter Paulina); after Paulina's death (c. 396/397) took the monk's profession while remaining in Rome; with Fabiola founded the travelers' hospice at Portus; the standing addressee of Jerome's most consequential defenses (Ep. 57, the Apology)

sources.locus: sec. 10 (the Portus hospice, founded with Fabiola)

records.bridge_line: the widow whose fortune and resolve built Bethlehem - founder and head of the women's community, mother of Eustochium and Blaesilla, the material foundation of the whole scholarly project

dates.died: 404, Bethlehem - Ep. 108 dates her death precisely and gives her age; buried by the Church of the Nativity
dates.floruit: Rome until 385 (widowed 379/380, ascetic under Marcella's circle's influence); the 385-386 journey; Bethlehem 386-404 (founder and head of the women's community)

records.bridge_line: the granddaughter vowed from the cradle - the child whose alphabet was designed by letter from Bethlehem, and who, still young, co-signed the community's report of the fire

dates.born: c. 397/400, Rome (approximate - Ep. 107 addresses her infancy c. 403)
dates.floruit: vowed to virginity from birth by her parents Laeta and Toxotius (Paula's son); the subject of Ep. 107's education program; at Bethlehem by 416, when she and her aunt Eustochium reported the attack to Pope Innocent

sources.locus: whole letter (the education program prescribed for her)
Ep. 137 (co-author, with Eustochium, of the lost report to Innocent)

records.bridge_line: the oldest friend who became the fiercest opponent - fellow translator of Origen, whose preface recalling Jerome's earlier admiration of the master set off the rupture neither man ever repaired

dates.died: 411, Sicily, in flight from the Gothic invasion
dates.floruit: Jerome's close friend from their student days; monastic founder on the Mount of Olives with Melania the Elder; translator of Origen into Latin - whose Peri Archon preface (397), describing without naming Jerome as Origen's earlier translator, ignited the public rupture; the exchange of Apologies 401-403

records.description: A running argument, carried by letter across a real distance, with a respected fellow scholar who would not simply concede the point: Augustine's objection that abandoning the Septuagint's received authority risked the church's continuity and unity, tested concretely when a congregation at Oea revolted over one changed word in Jonah. The external pressure under which the Hebraica veritas commitment was articulated, refined, and defended in real time.
manifestations: Augustine's Ep. 71 - the Oea incident and the plea for the Septuagint
Jerome's Ep. 112 - the point-by-point defense
the exchange's quarter-century span, misdirected letters and all
records.name: The Jerome-Augustine correspondence and the Latin scriptural-authority contest [2A - ongoing/external]

sources.locus: Epp. 71, 82 (the objection and the Oea report, his own hand)

records.description: An ongoing structural exposure: Jerome's Rome-period standing depended on the continued personal favor of one man - Pope Damasus's clerical protection, a different kind of patronage than Paula's material funding. The exposure became acute in 384: Blaesilla's death from ascetic excess brought public accusation against Jerome specifically; Damasus's death that December removed the shield; the resulting clerical hostility drove the August 385 departure. Favor held at one man's pleasure, and gone the moment that man was gone.
manifestations: the accusation and slander after Blaesilla's death, in Jerome's own reports
the December 384 loss of Damasus - protection, not funding, was what failed
the August 385 departure (Documented); a formal synod reviewing his conduct is NOT asserted (Inferential-Thin)
Paula's material funding chain holding throughout - what carried the project into relocation rather than destitution
records.name: Clerical-reputational precarity of Rome standing - the 384-385 crisis [2A - ongoing/external]

records.description: A trained scholar arriving with exactly the philological competence the Aventine circle had lacked: Jerome reaches Rome as secretary and scriptural adviser to Pope Damasus, and converges with Marcella's already-established household. Without this convergence there is no Hebrew-based translation project and no patronage-authority structure - the external half of the world's double origin.
manifestations: the Damasus commission to revise the Latin Gospels
the scriptural question-and-answer relationship with the Aventine circle, begun almost at once
records.name: Jerome's arrival in Rome with scholarly credentials [1A - initiating/external]

records.description: A widow who had already chosen, on her own initiative, the discipline that later became this world's shared practice - plain dress, fasting, scriptural study in her own house on the Aventine - before any outside teacher named or systematized it for her. The internal seed of the world: the household Jerome arrived INTO, not one he created.
manifestations: her refusal of remarriage to a man of consular rank, and the ascetic commitment that followed (dating to her early widowhood)
the household's growth into a gathering of like-minded women (its dating deliberately imprecise - no source gives a year)
the scriptural seriousness that later filled a dozen of Jerome's answering letters
records.name: Marcella's household reading practice, pre-Jerome [1B - initiating/internal]

sources.locus: secs. 3-5 (her turn to ascetic life; the household's practice)

records.description: A pattern of desert withdrawal and communal discipline, witnessed firsthand on the founding journey - Nitria's communities coming out with Bishop Isidore to meet Paula - carried back and adapted, not copied: Bethlehem's organization borrows the Egyptian devotional and organizational pattern while producing a distinctly Latin, literary variant.
manifestations: the 385-386 journey's attested Nitria encounter (Isidore and an unnamed monastic multitude - the famous desert-father names in the same passage are a rhetorical flourish, not a reception roster)
the two-household Bethlehem arrangement on a broadly Egyptian communal pattern
Jerome's later translation of the Pachomian Rule (c. 404) - a separate, later evidentiary thread, not part of the founding journey
records.name: The Egyptian/Palestinian monastic movement as institutional template [2A - ongoing/external]

sources.locus: sec. 14 (the Nitria encounter - Bishop Isidore and the unnamed multitude)

records.description: A doctrinal inheritance this world had absorbed without quite noticing, suddenly requiring urgent public renunciation: the dispute over Origen's teachings (c. 393-403) ruptured Jerome's oldest friendship (Rufinus) and set the community against its own bishop (John of Jerusalem). Internal in origin: the fracture ran through the community's own inheritance and relationships, not an outside attack.
manifestations: Rufinus's Peri Archon preface (397), describing without naming Jerome as Origen's earlier translator - the spark
the exchange of Apologies, 401-403, both surviving
the maneuvering around Bishop John of Jerusalem, under whose parish Bethlehem lay
Pammachius and Marcella as named addressees of Jerome's polemic - the dispute conducted through the patronage network itself
records.name: The Origenist controversy [2B - ongoing/internal]

records.description: A resilient pagan senatorial culture, and a wider Roman society, that read aristocratic renunciation as betrayal of family and rank: choosing this life invited real social judgment from one's own class - mockery, suspicion, and at the worst moment open hostility at a young woman's funeral. The force that made the renunciation-boundary genuinely costly to cross, not merely symbolic.
manifestations: the family resistance to Paula's divestment and departure (attested only through Jerome's own account - a structural silence, named)
the crowd's anger at Blaesilla's funeral, turned on the monks
the standing pagan senatorial culture (the Symmachus circle's Rome) as the class environment renunciation defied
records.name: Pagan-aristocratic and social backlash against renunciation [2A - ongoing/external]

sources.locus: secs. 2-4 (the slander and judgment he reports)
sec. 6 (the funeral crowd's muttering against the monks)

records.description: A theological argument that had, until then, stayed on paper, arriving instead as fire at the community's own door: the monasteries attacked and partly burned, deaths reported, the aging community scattered from its buildings. External by actor-origin (the classification the cleared documents settled); this world's own prior position-taking is part of why this force found this target - a genuine secondary observation that does not change the classification.
manifestations: the ravages, murders, and fires of Innocent's summary (Ep. 137, to John of Jerusalem) - reported to him by Eustochium and the younger Paula, whose own letter is lost
Jerome's brief, vague notices (Epp. 138-139 - his own house 'completely destroyed... so far as fleshly wealth is concerned')
no precision manufactured beyond what the sources hold (attackers' numbers and specific casualties are not attested)
records.name: The 416 attack on the Bethlehem monasteries [3A - ending/external]

records.description: A senatorial-class ascetic movement among Roman Christian women, already active before this world's own span opens - a movement this world's participants understood themselves as joining and extending, not founding from nothing. It established the social and devotional template (renunciation as aristocratic Christian practice) the whole formation ecology presupposes.
manifestations: Marcella's example followed first by Sophronia, then by others, in Jerome's own account
the wider senatorial renunciation pattern independently attested for this period
records.name: Roman aristocratic ascetic movement, pre-existing [1A - initiating/external]

sources.locus: secs. 4-5 (Marcella's early example followed by others)

records.description: Alaric's forces take Rome; Marcella's Aventine household is broken into, she is roughly handled by soldiers demanding treasure a household had already given away years before, and she dies soon after. The single clearest ending-force within the world's own span: it removes the Rome pole's independent center, and the world's final decade is Bethlehem-concentrated in a way its earlier decades were not.
manifestations: the soldiers in the house, and her reported calm (epitaph-genre detail, handled as such)
her death shortly after, with Principia beside her
the wider shock reaching Bethlehem - the world's own scholar mourning the city across the sea
records.name: The 410 Gothic sack of Rome [3A - ending/external]

sources.locus: secs. 12-14 (the sack; Marcella's treatment and death)

records.description: The praefatio/epistula apparatus - defending each translated book on its own terms, book by book, against live objection - had exactly one practitioner across the world's entire span. No successor scholar, editor, or defender of the method is attested anywhere in the record. After the last preface, no one remained who could write the next one in the same voice: the translation project passes from a live, actively defended argument into a fixed, undefended text, whose slow later reception proceeds without the mechanism that had shaped it.
manifestations: the absence itself - no successor named anywhere in the surviving record (an absence, not an inference)
the contrast with the sacramental and communal practices, which needed no single practitioner to persist
records.name: Transmission's end - the defense mechanism dies with its one practitioner [3B - ending/internal; named force]

sources.locus: the corpus's own shape - no successor's preface exists

records.description: How the ecology passed itself on within its own span: every finished piece of translation labor accompanied by its own defense, sent onward to the very households whose funding and whose questions had occasioned it - and outward to a wider Latin readership. The community's internal transmission mechanism, named as its own force per the transmission-specificity discipline, never folded into the general letter-writing gravity.
manifestations: the preface attached to nearly every translated book - argument as transmission
the dedications binding each work to Paula, Eustochium, Marcella, and their circle
the letters carrying direction, correction, and the community's own self-account from Bethlehem to Rome and beyond
records.name: Transmission - the praefatio/epistula apparatus [2B - ongoing/internal; named force]

records.description: Wealth, marriage prospects, and social rank deliberately unmade as Christian formation - the central content of the women's own asceticism and the material source of everything the world built. The strongest Formation-test result of any candidate for the women's half of the ecology: renunciation was not preparation for formation, it WAS the formation.
manifestations: Paula's divestment and her funding of the Bethlehem monasteries and hospice
Fabiola's fortune spent on the sick (the Roman hospital) and on the harbor hospice
Marcella's plain-dress, plain-food Aventine household, decades before Jerome arrived
the family resistance and public judgment the choice provoked - and, in Blaesilla's death, its most terrible cost
records.name: Voluntary ascetic self-impoverishment [PRIMARY]

records.description: Doctrinal and textual dispute as an organizing pressure across nearly the whole span: the Origenist rupture (393-403), the running Hebrew/Septuagint contest with Augustine, and the Pelagian conflict that ended in the 416 attack. Supporting rather than Primary: the ecology's organized response to pressures on its Primary commitments, not an independent formation practice of its own.
manifestations: the exchange of Apologies with Rufinus - both sides surviving in their own words
the community defining itself against Origen's contested conclusions after absorbing his methods
the 416 attack - argument arrived as fire
Jerome's combative self-presentation, formed by and forming the disputes
records.name: Controversy as formation-shaping pressure [SUPPORTING]

records.description: The letter as the community's actual formation apparatus: spiritual direction delivered, scriptural argument conducted, and a community physically split between Rome and Bethlehem held together as one project for decades. Supporting rather than Primary: an enabling MEDIUM through which the Primary gravities operate, not an independent force generating its own formation content - and its overwhelming attestation is partly an artifact of the source base itself being letters.
manifestations: Ep. 22's direction of Eustochium's formation, delivered as a letter
the Marcella question-and-answer series - a dozen-plus scriptural consultations in two Rome years
the Bethlehem commentaries dedicated and dispatched to Rome, book by book
the Augustine dispute, conducted entirely by letter across the sea
records.name: Letter-writing as formation medium [SUPPORTING]

records.description: The conviction that the Hebrew text of scripture carries the truth closest to its inspired origin, held and practiced as a formation commitment: the whole translation project, the years of Hebrew study, and the running public defense of both. CLASSIFICATION BASIS: Primary on the attestation-level evidence (the translation artifact exists; the dispute is independently attested in Augustine's own hand); the separate Contested question of Jerome's actual Hebrew fluency does not lower the gravity's organizing strength and is carried as its own contest, not dissolved.
manifestations: the translation project itself, from the Damasus-commissioned Gospels revision to the Hebrew Old Testament rendered book by book at Bethlehem
the praefatio practice - each book defended on arrival against live objection
the Augustine correspondence and the Oea congregation's revolt over one changed word
Hebrew study under Jewish teachers, paid for by Paula's patronage
records.name: Hebraica veritas - Hebrew-based textual authority [PRIMARY]

records.statement: You ask what it was to be enslaved among us. Our record is silent. The great households held many people, and our writings never let one of them speak, or even gave one a name.
records.why_sources_cannot_answer: The senatorial households at the center of this world - Paula's, Marcella's, Fabiola's - necessarily included enslaved and dependent people, and their lives were reorganized by their patrons' renunciations (households broken up, fortunes redirected). Not one such person appears in the sources as a subject: no name, no voice, no account of what a mistress's conversion meant for those she owned. The elite, literate character of everything that survives makes this a structural silence, not an archival accident.

sources.locus: secs. 14, 34 (the buildings named; the burial by the church)

records.statement: If you dug where we lived, we cannot tell you what you would find. No stone, coin, or record of ours has been traced with certainty. What is known of our daily life comes from letters, not from the ground.
records.why_sources_cannot_answer: No papyri, inscriptions, administrative records, or excavated structures specific to the Bethlehem monasteries, the women's community, or the hospice have been identified; later building at the Nativity site complicates its archaeology, and any claim tying particular remains to these communities is thin. How historians know this world at all is the other half of the honest answer: through an unusually rich literary survival - the letters and prefaces - which is also the only survival.

sources.locus: sec. 7 (her questions attested, her letters lost)
whole letter (the one letter in their names - held to be his)

records.statement: You ask for the women's own words. We must be honest: not one written word of theirs was kept. They wrote - questions, letters, a report of the fire that reached a pope - and every page is lost. What remains is what one man wrote about them.
records.why_sources_cannot_answer: No text composed by Paula, Eustochium, Marcella, or Fabiola survives. The women demonstrably wrote: Jerome's surviving letters answer Marcella's written questions by the dozen, and Pope Innocent's reply attests the report Eustochium and the younger Paula sent after the attack on the monasteries. The one letter transmitted under the women's names is widely accepted as Jerome's own composition for them. The absence is a fact of transmission - who curated what was kept - not a fact about the women.

sources.locus: Ep. 137 ('murders' - the community's only violent deaths, unnamed)

records.statement: We must answer plainly: the great persecutions ended before our time, and we have no martyr stories of our own. The account you name of tortured slave women belongs to an earlier age of the church, not to us. Our own dead fell in one attack by fellow Christians, and even their names were not kept.
records.why_sources_cannot_answer: This world's span falls after the persecutions: no member was martyred by a hostile empire, no martyr-acts belong to its own record, and the outside-account-under-torture question (Pliny's interrogation of the two enslaved women) concerns the church of three centuries earlier, about which this world is not a witness. The desire-for-martyrdom question likewise has no object here: this world's costly deaths were an ascetic daughter's and a raid's victims', and its record treats both as grief, not as sought glory. An honest voice for this world can discuss martyrdom only as inherited memory and hagiographic ideal, never from its own experience.

records.tellable_as: the attack on the Bethlehem monasteries in the world's last years, as far as the record actually tells it
records.text: Near the end, the argument came to the doors. Men attacked the monasteries at Bethlehem - the record speaks of ravages, murders, fires, and outrages of all kinds; buildings burned; the old scholar wrote afterward, briefly, that his own monastery had been destroyed and that he had chosen to leave his pleasant home rather than surrender the faith. It was Eustochium and her young niece Paula who wrote to the bishop of Rome and told him what had been done. Writing on to the bishop of Jerusalem about it, Rome's bishop marveled that the women, in their own report, had declined to name the man behind it. He also wrote his sympathy to Jerome directly, and a rebuke to the bishop of Jerusalem for letting it happen. Who struck the blow, how many died, what was lost - the community itself chose not to say, and its restraint is most of what survives.

records.absent_detail: Whether the dream happened as told - or at all, as more than a literary conversion-scene - cannot be established; Rufinus later mocked him with exactly that question, and with the oath's apparent breach. What the story reliably attests is the tension it dramatizes: this world loved the polish of pagan letters and the plainness of scripture with the same trained ear, and it never made the two loves easy together.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 3 (attributed tradition): an autobiographical dream-vision embedded in an exhortatory letter - a recognized rhetorical and spiritual device of the age; the tension it dramatizes is widely accepted as a real, lived formation tension, while the dream as a literally-reported event is thin.

records.tellable_as: Jerome's dream of the Judge - the war between the books he loved and the book he served, as he himself told it
records.text: He told the story against himself, in a letter meant to teach. On the way to his desert years he could give up everything, he said, except his library. He fasted - and then read Cicero. He wept over his sins - and then picked up his beloved authors again; and when he made himself return to the prophets, their style seemed rough and unpolished after all that marble prose. Then, in a fever so deep his funeral was being prepared, he was dragged in spirit before the judgment seat. Asked who he was, he answered: a Christian. And the Judge said: you lie - you are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ; for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. He was flogged, he said - but worse was his conscience burning; and he swore an oath that if he ever again possessed worldly books he would have denied his Lord. He woke with his eyes drenched, and gave himself to the divine books - he tells us - with more zeal than he had ever given to the books of men. He kept telling this story his whole life. His enemies later noted, not unfairly, that his pages never did stop quoting the classics.

records.absent_detail: The schedule itself: which hours, which psalms, how the men's and women's worship divided - not attested; the women's regimen is one letter's memorial summary, the men's is a visitor's sketch of one man. The unnamed members of both houses - their number aside from one uncorroborated headcount, their names, their own days - are absent from every source, and this reconstruction does not invent them.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 4 (historically grounded reconstruction): no single source narrates a specific day; this is explicitly a composite of typical practice from attested elements only - the general fact of a structured common life, psalmody at set times, wool-work, the reading and copying labor, the hospice traffic - with no liturgical timetable supplied, because none is attested.

records.tellable_as: a typical day among the Bethlehem communities, offered openly as reconstruction from the letters' scattered notices, never as a documented schedule
records.text: Put together, from scattered notices, a typical day might be told like this - and told only like this, as a putting-together. The women rose before light for psalms; they met for the psalter at set times through the day and returned to their quarters between, to prayer, to the scriptures each was required to learn, and to wool-work - senators' daughters at the distaff, dressed alike in coarse cloth. They ate sparely; the sick among them were made to eat more, and were nursed. No man came among them; an offending sister was corrected and, stubborn, prayed back into the fold. Across the way, the men's house kept its own round of prayer and labor - and at its center, by every account, one old man was always at his books, day and night, reading or writing something, dictating letters that would cross the sea, working through the prophets with visitors from three provinces waiting. Pilgrims came and went at the hospice below. What the bells and hours precisely were, no one wrote down - or nothing that was written survived.

records.tellable_as: the desert hero-tales Bethlehem wrote - Malchus the captive and Hilarion the wonder-worker - told as the stories this world told, not as history
records.text: At Bethlehem, between translations, the scholar wrote adventure stories - holy ones. He told of Malchus, a monk carried off by desert raiders, enslaved, forced into a marriage he would not consummate, who fled across the river on inflated skins and hid in a cave while a lioness dispatched his pursuer - and came home still chaste. He told of Hilarion, who took the desert discipline to Palestine and could not outrun his own fame - crowds, miracles, demons shrieking out of the possessed - a hermit hunted by admirers from Gaza to Sicily to Cyprus, seeking only to be left alone with God. These were written to be read aloud, wept over, imitated. This world's people knew Roman romances; these were their answer - the same thrills, aimed at heaven. Whether the adventures happened is another matter, and even in that day some asked.

records.absent_detail: The telling is Jerome's epitaph for Paula, written for her daughter - idealizing by genre; her dry eyes and her words at the manger are his report. The famous desert-father names invoked in the Nitria passage are a rhetorical flourish, not a reception roster (one of the men named did not reach the desert until years after her visit); only Bishop Isidore and an unnamed monastic multitude are attested as met. No itinerary date, ship, or route detail beyond the letter's sequence is attested.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 1 (documented historical narrative): named author (Jerome), datable (composed 404, describing 385-386), near-contemporary, historically credible in broad outline - though single-sourced and authored by an interested party; scene-level details carry lower confidence than the narrative frame (the reviewed finding on the Nitria passage's rhetorical name-list is carried in absent_detail).

records.tellable_as: the journey of Paula and Jerome from Rome to the Holy Land and Egypt, and the choice to stay at Bethlehem, as the community itself recorded it
records.text: In the year after the troubles in Rome, Paula went down to the harbor with her children on the shore. The account says her eyes were dry, held toward heaven, as the ship pulled out - her little son stretching out his hands from the beach. She sailed east by way of Cyprus, where the bishop Epiphanius received her; then to Antioch; then down the whole length of the holy places, scripture in hand at every stop - and at the cave in Bethlehem she wept and greeted the town by name, the house of bread where the Bread from heaven was born. She went on into Egypt, to Nitria, where the bishop Isidore came out to meet her with a great crowd of monks. She wished to press deeper into the desert and stay among the monastic settlements; instead she turned back to Bethlehem, and there - in a small lodging at first, then in the monasteries her fortune built - she stayed for the rest of her life. The journey ended not in seeing the places but in never leaving them.

records.absent_detail: The scene reaches Jerome at second hand ('what I have heard... what holy men have seen'), two years after the event, in a genre built to exemplify; her felt-no- pain composure and her thanksgiving are the epitaph's conventions doing their work. No independent account of her death exists. Even here, at her most remembered, her own words are reported, not preserved.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 1 for the core event (Marcella died following the sack of Rome - near-contemporary, named author, written to an eyewitness), with the scene-level detail explicitly flagged as epitaph-genre reporting at second hand (Jerome writes 'be it mine to say what I have heard').

records.tellable_as: Marcella's last hours in the sack of Rome, as Jerome heard and recorded them
records.text: When the Goths broke into Rome, the soldiers came at last to the house on the Aventine. The old woman received them, the account says, without a look of alarm; when they demanded her gold she pointed to her coarse dress - a household that had already given its treasure away years before. They did not believe her. They beat her with cudgels. She is said to have felt no pain, but to have thrown herself at their feet pleading - not for herself, but that they spare the young woman in her care. Something in the scene reached even those men; they took the two women to the basilica of the apostle Paul, where Marcella had hoped they might find safety or, failing that, at least a grave together. Marcella lived a short while longer - long enough, the account says, to give thanks that she died with her poverty complete and Rome's agony only beginning behind her. Far away in Bethlehem, the man who had answered her scripture questions for thirty years wrote her memorial with his voice sticking in his throat.

records.absent_detail: The consultations, their frequency, the clergy's deference, her role against the heretics - all rest on Ep. 127 alone, post-mortem, in a letter partly serving its author's own vindication; her deference-form (opinions given as from a teacher) may be her prudence, the age's constraint on women teaching, or his framing. Her own letters and her own exegesis were not kept. This story must never be told as documented fact about the extent of her authority - only as the world's own remembered account of it, with the frame named.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 3 (attributed tradition): attributed to a specific figure in a commemorative-genre account authored after her death for purposes modern analysis reads as partly self-vindicating; the single most author-gravity-constrained story in this inventory, usable only with its single-source, post-mortem framing spoken every time.

records.tellable_as: the standing Marcella held in Rome, as the one account of it tells it - named always as one man's memorial claim
records.text: Long before the famous scholar came to Rome, there was a widow on the Aventine hill who had refused a rich old suitor with the words that had she wished to marry again she would have sought a husband, not an inheritance. When the scholar arrived, she besieged him with scripture questions until his reluctance gave way; and she never accepted an answer without disputing it - not to argue, he wrote later, but to learn what could be said against every answer. When he left for Bethlehem, the memorial says, something remarkable remained behind: if a dispute arose in Rome about the testimony of scripture, it was to her house that they came - clergy among them, priests among them - and she settled it. She gave her opinions, he adds, as if they were not her own but a teacher's, mindful of the apostle's rule. And at the end of her life she was, in his telling, the one who set in motion the condemnation of the heretics in Rome. All of this is one man's memorial of her, written when she was two years dead. The letters she wrote him are lost. The learning is certain - a dozen of his surviving answers attest the quality of her questions. The rest is his word.

records.absent_detail: The incident reaches us only through Augustine's summary (and Jerome's reply to it): the bishop of Oea is unnamed, the date is approximate, and the Jewish residents' actual answer about the Hebrew survives only in Augustine's report of the bishop's report - with Augustine's own aside ('whether from ignorance or spite') showing the layers of hearsay even the ancient account admits.
records.narrative_tier_justification: Tier 1 (documented historical narrative): two named authors, both sides of the exchange surviving independently in their own collections - the rare story in this inventory where the other side is not lost.

retrieve_when: what the translation project cost in real congregations
